1	---
2	name: pulse-factory
3	description: Arm a Pulse Factory run for a planned spine, propose a start from the Orchestrator chat, read its status, and halt it. Use when the operator asks to run a spine unattended, to start a run on Pulse Factory, to see what a run costs, or to stop one.
4	---
5	
6	# Pulse Factory
7	
8	Pulse Factory runs the seats of a planned spine with no model session watching. You arm a run once.
9	A controller (a systemd user service) then drives the seats until each item PR has merged into the
10	spine branch. A spine-close seat then opens the spine PR, and the PR merges into the base branch
11	only on your ack. The CLI contract is `docs/contracts/cli.md`. This skill covers the verbs: `arm`,
12	`propose`, which posts a start card into the Orchestrator chat, `status`, `halt`, `hook` and
13	`controller`, the verbs of requests and the claim: `requests`, `show`, `claim`, `answer`, `clear`
14	and `ack`, `project`, which lists the operator's projects, `session`, which chats with a project's
15	Orchestrator, `settings`, which reads and sets the chat policies, `chat-runtime`, which installs the
16	runtime that chat needs, and `device` and `api`, which pair and revoke the devices that reach the
17	controller over the network.
18	
19	## Arm a run
20	
21	1. Work out the `--param` values with the planning method's own tool. The binary never calls that
22	   tool. Run the commands in a code block like this one, and read their output:
23	
24	   ```bash
25	   # The spine branch, the spine directory, the repo and the method's root. Adapt the names to
26	   # your method; the workflow file lists the parameters it declares.
27	   method_root="$(pwd)"
28	   spine=r0.s1
29	   release="$(oss get ".spines[] | select(.id == \"$spine\") | .release")"
30	   name="$(oss get ".spines[] | select(.id == \"$spine\") | .name")"
31	   slug="$(printf '%s' "$name" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | sed 's/[^a-z0-9]\{1,\}/-/g; s/^-//; s/-$//')"
32	   spine_branch="$(oss branch_name "$spine" "$slug")"
33	   spine_dir="$method_root/$(oss spine_dir "$release" "$spine" "$slug")"
34	   plugin_root="$HOME/.claude/plugins/cache"
35	   # The branch the spine PR merges into. The method recorded it when the spine started.
36	   base_branch="$(oss spine_base_get "$spine" "$(basename "$PWD")")"
37	   ```
38	
39	   `spine_base_get` takes the spine and the repo name as the method's state records it. Use that
40	   name if it is not the directory name.
41	
42	2. Show the plan first. A dry run reads and checks. It starts nothing and records nothing:
43	
44	   ```bash
45	   pulse-factory arm "$spine" --workflow ossify-spine --ledger "$spine_dir/autopilot-ledger.md" \
46	     --plugin-root "$plugin_root" \
47	     --param spine_branch="$spine_branch" --param spine_dir="$spine_dir" \
48	     --param repo="$PWD" --param method_root="$method_root" \
49	     --param worktree_root="$PWD/.worktrees" --param state_file="$method_root/.state.json" \
50	     --param oss="$(command -v oss)" --param base_branch="$base_branch" \
51	     --dry-run
52	   ```
53	
54	   Every `--param` value must be an absolute path or plain text. The controller runs in another
55	   directory, so a value that is `.` or starts with `./` or `../` is refused.
56	
57	3. Read the summary to the operator: the spine, the item count, each role with its model, the caps,
58	   the pinned plugins, the most launches the run can make, and two merge lines: item PRs merge into
59	   the spine branch on green checks with no ack, and the spine PR merges into the base branch only
60	   on the claim's ack. The operator approves what they saw.
61	
62	4. Start the run with the same command and `--yes` in place of `--dry-run`. It prints the run ID.
63	   Add `--replace <run>` to replace an earlier run that has no running session.
64	
65	`arm` refuses with a cause and records nothing when the plan is wrong. A refusal is not an error to
66	work around: tell the operator the cause.
67	
68	This is the operator's CLI path. A chat process, and anything that descends from one, is refused on
69	`arm`. A chat proposes the start instead (next section).
70	
71	## Propose a start from the Orchestrator chat
72	
73	The Orchestrator chat starts nothing by itself. It posts a **start card** into its own chat, and the
74	operator confirms the card on a paired device. Only then does the run arm.
75	
76	1. Work out the `--param` values as in step 1 of "Arm a run".
77	2. Run `propose` with the spine and the same inputs as `arm`. It has no `--replace` and no `--yes`.
78	   `--workflow` takes the name of an installed workflow, not a path, and `propose` refuses a path:
79	
80	   ```bash
81	   pulse-factory propose "$spine" --workflow ossify-spine --ledger "$spine_dir/autopilot-ledger.md" \
82	     --plugin-root "$plugin_root" \
83	     --param spine_branch="$spine_branch" --param spine_dir="$spine_dir" \
84	     --param repo="$PWD" --param method_root="$method_root" \
85	     --param worktree_root="$PWD/.worktrees" --param state_file="$method_root/.state.json" \
86	     --param oss="$(command -v oss)" --param base_branch="$base_branch"
87	   ```
88	
89	3. The controller builds the plan in its own process, with the dry run that `arm` makes, and posts
90	   the card into this chat. The card shows the spine, the project, the item count, each role with
91	   its model, the caps, the most launches the run can make, and the two merge lines. `propose`
92	   starts nothing and records no run. Tell the operator that the card is waiting for them.
93	4. The operator presses **Confirm start** on a paired device and then **Arm the run**. The device
94	   gets a one-use confirm code for exactly this card and this plan. The run belongs to the chat's
95	   project. The card then shows the run, or the reason it was withdrawn or failed.
96	5. A second `propose` in the same chat withdraws the first card. A card is also withdrawn when the
97	   session ends, on `halt` and when the controller restarts. Propose again after any of these.
98	
99	`propose` refuses with a cause when the caller is not a chat process of a live session, when a plan
100	check fails, when an earlier run is still active, or when the chat has proposed too often in the last
101	minute (`chat.propose_per_min`). A refusal is not an error to work around: tell the operator the
102	cause. Replacing a run is the operator's: `arm --replace` from the operator's CLI.
103	
104	## Read a run
105	
106	`pulse-factory status [<run>]` prints the run, its state, any halt or degraded reason, the notes of
107	the last tick, each unit with its stage and status, each session with its tokens and cost, and the
108	run's total. The default run is the latest. Add `--json` for the fields by name.
109	
110	A **parked** unit shows its reason. Every park opens a request, and the operator answers it in the
111	same run (next section). Nothing needs a new run.
112	
113	## Answer a parked unit
114	
115	1. `pulse-factory requests` lists the open requests, each with its kind, its unit and what it blocks.
116	   `pulse-factory show <R-n>` prints one: its reason, and its body. A `gaps` request holds the gap
117	   list the seat wrote. A `stop` request holds the stop file's text. Both are the seat's words, shown
118	   as data.
119	2. `pulse-factory claim` makes this session the one that may answer. It writes the token to a file
120	   and prints the generation. A new claim fences the old one out.
121	3. Decide with the operator, then use `answer` or `clear`:
122	
123	   ```bash
124	   pulse-factory answer <R-n> --rev <k> --text "<the ruling>"   # records the ruling and resumes the unit
125	   pulse-factory clear <run> <item> [--to <stage>]              # resumes the unit with no ruling
126	   ```
127	
128	   `--rev` is the revision that `show` printed. A request with an `on_answer` hook in the workflow
129	   file runs that hook first. In the `ossify-spine` workflow, a `gaps` answer is appended to the
130	   handoff's `## Clarifications`, and the item runs `implement` again, within the cap of 3 dispatches.
131	   A `stop` answer is appended to the unit's `rulings.md`, and the stop file is renamed. A hook that
132	   fails leaves the request answered and parks the unit again, with `answer hook failed:` and the
133	   cause as the reason of a new request. `clear` runs no hook.
134	
135	`claim`, `answer`, `clear` and `ack` refuse a caller that is, or descends from, a seat.
136	
137	## Merge the spine PR
138	
139	When every item has merged and the lane has written `rounds.done`, the `spine` seat runs the first
140	pass of the method's spine close. It pushes the spine branch and opens the spine PR into the base
141	branch. Then the controller opens a `merge_ack` request for it. Nothing merges until the claim
142	holder acks.
143	
144	1. `pulse-factory requests` lists the `merge_ack` request. `pulse-factory show <R-n>` prints the PR,
145	   the base branch, the head branch and the head SHA the ack will merge. Check them against the
146	   forge. Review the PR and drive it to a mergeable state as you would any PR.
147	2. `pulse-factory claim`, if this session does not hold the claim.
148	3. `pulse-factory ack <R-n> --rev <k>`, with the revision that `show` printed. The controller reads
149	   the PR again. If the head moved, it revises the request to the new SHA and refuses; `show` the
150	   request and ack the new revision. If the checks are not green, or the PR has a conflict, or the
151	   base or head branch changed, it refuses with the cause and the request stays open. Otherwise it
152	   merges the PR with that SHA pinned, then fetches the base branch.
153	4. After the merge, run the second pass in your own session or in the project's Orchestrator chat:
154	   `/ossify:close <spine>` on Claude Code, `skill://close <spine>` on OMP. It finds the merged PR and records the close, runs the
155	   demo and runs the harvest. A seat does not run it. The run ends when the method records the
156	   spine as closed, and `status` shows each session's cost and the run's total.
157	
158	`ack` answers only a `merge_ack` request. `answer` and `clear` refuse one and name `ack`. A merge
159	that does not land parks the unit with a `merge_failed` request. `clear` sends it back to the merge,
160	which opens a new `merge_ack`. A halted or ended run refuses the ack.
161	
162	## Register a project
163	
164	A project is a directory the operator works in: a git repo or a plain folder. It has an ID, a name
165	and one root, and nothing more yet. These verbs launch nothing and change no run.
166	
167	```bash
168	pulse-factory project add ~/projects/pulse-factory            # project P-1 added: pulse-factory (…)
169	pulse-factory project add ./notes --name "Field notes"        # a relative root is taken from here
170	pulse-factory project list                                    # P-1  pulse-factory  <HOME>
171	pulse-factory project remove P-2                              # the row stays; the ID is not reused
172	```
173	
174	1. `project add <root>` records the root, made canonical, under a name. The name is the root's last
175	   component unless `--name` gives one. A missing path, a file, `/`, a root that a live project holds
176	   already, and a name that a live project holds already are refused, each with its reason. A root
177	   that is a linked worktree (add its main worktree instead), a bare repository, the inside of a
178	   `.git` directory and a repository that git refuses for dubious ownership are refused too, with
179	   the cause.
180	2. `project list` shows the live projects in creation order. `--json` gives
181	   `{"schema_version": 1, "projects": [...]}`.
182	3. A retry of `add` or `remove` sends the same `--command-id`. The controller admits the command
183	   once and returns the first record, with `"replayed": true`. With no `--command-id`, each call
184	   makes a random one.
185	
186	Every `add` and `remove`, admitted or refused, is one line of `<state dir>/controller.ledger`. A seat
187	cannot `add` or `remove`; it can `list`.
188	
189	## Chat with a project's Orchestrator
190	
191	Each project has a built-in Orchestrator: a Claude Code chat that runs in the project's main worktree
192	on this server. You start it, send it messages, answer its approvals and questions, and end it. No
193	verb waits for a reply: a verb sends one request, prints one answer and exits. You read the chat with
194	`session items`, and the app reads it on the API stream.
195	
196	```bash
197	pulse-factory session start --project P-1            # session S-1 started in <HOME> (worktree W-1)
198	pulse-factory session send S-1 "what is open?"       # sent to S-1
199	pulse-factory session items S-1                      # one line for each item, after --after <seq>
200	pulse-factory session answer S-1 4 --deny "not now"  # or --allow, or --answer "<question>=<label>"
201	pulse-factory session set S-1 --effort medium        # this chat only; the agent's defaults stay
202	pulse-factory session interrupt S-1                  # ends the running turn
203	pulse-factory session list                           # the live sessions, with their holders and cost
204	pulse-factory session end S-1                        # stops the process and ends the session
205	pulse-factory session redact S-1 4                   # redacts one stored item; CLI only
206	```
207	
208	1. `chat-runtime install` fetches the managed Claude Code copy at the pinned version. The install
209	   script runs it. A start before it is refused with a message that names it.
210	2. `session start` opens the process at once. The chat uses no token until you send a message. A
211	   second live Orchestrator for one project is refused, and the refusal names the live `S-<n>`.
212	3. `session send` opens the process again when it was released or stopped, and resumes the same
213	   conversation. A turn begins only on your message or when a background task the chat started
214	   finishes. The chat cannot wake itself: no timer, tick or notice starts a turn.
215	4. A process with no running turn, no background task and no pending request is released after 30
216	   idle minutes. The next `send` resumes it. The cap is `PF_CHAT_MAX_LIVE` (default 4). A refused
217	   open names every live chat and why it holds its process.
218	5. `session answer <S-n> <seq>` answers the pending approval or question whose item has that `seq`,
219	   which `session items` shows.
220	6. A session marked `context lost` cannot resume: end it and start a new one. `halt` stops every
221	   live chat process, and each session stays live; the next `send` reopens it.
222	7. A seat, and a chat process or anything that descends from one, cannot run the state-changing
223	   `session` verbs. `session list` and `session items` are reads. A paired device calls `session
224	   list`, `start`, `send`, `answer`, `interrupt`, `set` and `end`; `redact`, `items` and `halt` are
225	   not open to it.
226	
227	Every state-changing verb is one line of `<state dir>/controller.ledger`, and each process open,
228	turn and stop is one line of `<state dir>/chat.ledger`. A `send` line holds the byte count and never
229	the text.
230	
231	## Read and set chat policies
232	
233	`pulse-factory settings get [<key>] [--project P-n] [--agent <id>]` prints the value of a chat
234	policy for a context, with the scope it comes from. A chat reads its own policies this way.
235	
236	```bash
237	pulse-factory settings get                                  # one line for each key
238	pulse-factory settings get chat.propose_per_min --project P-1
239	pulse-factory settings set chat.self_turn_cap 5 --project P-1   # the operator's CLI or a device
240	pulse-factory settings unset chat.self_turn_cap --project P-1
241	```
242	
243	1. The keys are `chat.self_turn_cap`, `chat.deny_commands` and `chat.propose_per_min`. The last one
244	   bounds the proposals one chat session may build in a minute. It is a whole number from 0 to 60,
245	   the built-in value is 4, and `0` turns the bound off.
246	2. `settings set` and `settings unset` are the operator's: the CLI, and a paired device. A chat
247	   process, and anything that descends from one, is refused on both. Tell the operator what you
248	   want changed, and let them change it.
249	3. A retry of `set` or `unset` sends the same `--command-id`, as for `project`.
250	
251	## Pair a device
252	
253	The controller can serve a network API over TLS (ADR-0012). It is off until the operator sets
254	`PF_API_LISTEN` (`docs/install.md`). A paired device calls the project verbs, the chat verbs, `requests`,
255	`show`, `confirm_code`, `answer`, `clear`, `ack`, the settings verbs and `arm` with a confirm code
256	from a start card. `claim` and `halt` stay off it. It reads a chat on the stream
257	(`docs/contracts/api.md`).
258	
259	```bash
260	pulse-factory api status          # off | waiting for <addr> | listening on <addr> | failed: <why>
261	pulse-factory device pair         # prints one code, and when it stops working
262	pulse-factory device list         # D-1  <name>  paired …  last seen … from <peer>
263	pulse-factory device revoke D-1   # the device's next call is refused
264	```
265	
266	1. `device pair` prints one `pf1-` code. It works once, it expires after 10 minutes, and a new code
267	   replaces the live one. The code is a secret: give it to the operator, who types it into the
268	   device. Do not write it to a file, a ledger, a request or a message to anyone else.
269	2. `device list` shows each device with its pairing time, its last call and the peer address of that
270	   call. A revoked device is listed last, with its revoke time. `--json` gives
271	   `{"schema_version": 1, "devices": [...]}`. A record never holds a token.
272	3. `device revoke <id>` refuses that device's next call at once. The device pairs again with a new
273	   code. A retry sends the same `--command-id`, as for `project`.
274	4. `api status` says whether the API is `off`, `waiting for` an address that is not on the host yet,
275	   `listening on` it, or `failed`. It also prints the SPKI hash of the server key. A lost key means
276	   a new hash: revoke every device and pair again.
277	
278	Each `device pair` redeem and each `device revoke` is one line of `<state dir>/controller.ledger`.
279	The line names the device and never the code or the token. A seat cannot run `device pair` or
280	`device revoke`; `device list` and `api status` are reads.
281	
282	## Halt a run
283	
284	`pulse-factory halt [<run>] --reason "<why>"` stops new launches and new merges. Seats that run
285	finish their stage. A repeat is safe, and the first reason stays. `halt` also stops every live chat
286	process and answers with the sessions it stopped (see "Chat with a project's Orchestrator").
287	
288	## Other verbs
289	
290	- `pulse-factory controller` runs the controller in the foreground. The systemd user unit runs it.
291	  You do not run it yourself.
292	- `pulse-factory hook` judges one tool call of a seat. The seat's extension runs it. You do not run
293	  it yourself.
294	
295	A seat cannot arm or halt a run, it cannot add or remove a project, it cannot start or drive a chat,
296	and it cannot pair or revoke a device: those verbs refuse when `PF_SEAT_TOKEN` is set. A chat cannot
297	arm a run or change a setting: it proposes the start and the operator confirms it.
298

---
name: pulse-factory
description: Arm a Pulse Factory run for a planned spine, propose a start from the Orchestrator chat, read its status, and halt it. Use when the operator asks to run a spine unattended, to start a run on Pulse Factory, to see what a run costs, or to stop one.
---

# Pulse Factory

Pulse Factory runs the seats of a planned spine with no model session watching. You arm a run once.
A controller (a systemd user service) then drives the seats until each item PR has merged into the
spine branch. A spine-close seat then opens the spine PR, and the PR merges into the base branch
only on your ack. The CLI contract is `docs/contracts/cli.md`. This skill covers the verbs: `arm`,
`propose`, which posts a start card into the Orchestrator chat, `status`, `halt`, `hook` and
`controller`, the verbs of requests and the claim: `requests`, `show`, `claim`, `answer`, `clear`
and `ack`, `project`, which lists the operator's projects, `session`, which chats with a project's
Orchestrator, `settings`, which reads and sets the chat policies, `chat-runtime`, which installs the
runtime that chat needs, and `device` and `api`, which pair and revoke the devices that reach the
controller over the network.

## Arm a run

1. Work out the `--param` values with the planning method's own tool. The binary never calls that
   tool. Run the commands in a code block like this one, and read their output:

   ```bash
   # The spine branch, the spine directory, the repo and the method's root. Adapt the names to
   # your method; the workflow file lists the parameters it declares.
   method_root="$(pwd)"
   spine=r0.s1
   release="$(oss get ".spines[] | select(.id == \"$spine\") | .release")"
   name="$(oss get ".spines[] | select(.id == \"$spine\") | .name")"
   slug="$(printf '%s' "$name" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | sed 's/[^a-z0-9]\{1,\}/-/g; s/^-//; s/-$//')"
   spine_branch="$(oss branch_name "$spine" "$slug")"
   spine_dir="$method_root/$(oss spine_dir "$release" "$spine" "$slug")"
   plugin_root="$HOME/.claude/plugins/cache"
   # The branch the spine PR merges into. The method recorded it when the spine started.
   base_branch="$(oss spine_base_get "$spine" "$(basename "$PWD")")"
   ```

   `spine_base_get` takes the spine and the repo name as the method's state records it. Use that
   name if it is not the directory name.

2. Show the plan first. A dry run reads and checks. It starts nothing and records nothing:

   ```bash
   pulse-factory arm "$spine" --workflow ossify-spine --ledger "$spine_dir/autopilot-ledger.md" \
     --plugin-root "$plugin_root" \
     --param spine_branch="$spine_branch" --param spine_dir="$spine_dir" \
     --param repo="$PWD" --param method_root="$method_root" \
     --param worktree_root="$PWD/.worktrees" --param state_file="$method_root/.state.json" \
     --param oss="$(command -v oss)" --param base_branch="$base_branch" \
     --dry-run
   ```

   Every `--param` value must be an absolute path or plain text. The controller runs in another
   directory, so a value that is `.` or starts with `./` or `../` is refused.

3. Read the summary to the operator: the spine, the item count, each role with its model, the caps,
   the pinned plugins, the most launches the run can make, and two merge lines: item PRs merge into
   the spine branch on green checks with no ack, and the spine PR merges into the base branch only
   on the claim's ack. The operator approves what they saw.

4. Start the run with the same command and `--yes` in place of `--dry-run`. It prints the run ID.
   Add `--replace <run>` to replace an earlier run that has no running session.

`arm` refuses with a cause and records nothing when the plan is wrong. A refusal is not an error to
work around: tell the operator the cause.

This is the operator's CLI path. A chat process, and anything that descends from one, is refused on
`arm`. A chat proposes the start instead (next section).

## Propose a start from the Orchestrator chat

The Orchestrator chat starts nothing by itself. It posts a **start card** into its own chat, and the
operator confirms the card on a paired device. Only then does the run arm.

1. Work out the `--param` values as in step 1 of "Arm a run".
2. Run `propose` with the spine and the same inputs as `arm`. It has no `--replace` and no `--yes`.
   `--workflow` takes the name of an installed workflow, not a path, and `propose` refuses a path:

   ```bash
   pulse-factory propose "$spine" --workflow ossify-spine --ledger "$spine_dir/autopilot-ledger.md" \
     --plugin-root "$plugin_root" \
     --param spine_branch="$spine_branch" --param spine_dir="$spine_dir" \
     --param repo="$PWD" --param method_root="$method_root" \
     --param worktree_root="$PWD/.worktrees" --param state_file="$method_root/.state.json" \
     --param oss="$(command -v oss)" --param base_branch="$base_branch"
   ```

3. The controller builds the plan in its own process, with the dry run that `arm` makes, and posts
   the card into this chat. The card shows the spine, the project, the item count, each role with
   its model, the caps, the most launches the run can make, and the two merge lines. `propose`
   starts nothing and records no run. Tell the operator that the card is waiting for them.
4. The operator presses **Confirm start** on a paired device and then **Arm the run**. The device
   gets a one-use confirm code for exactly this card and this plan. The run belongs to the chat's
   project. The card then shows the run, or the reason it was withdrawn or failed.
5. A second `propose` in the same chat withdraws the first card. A card is also withdrawn when the
   session ends, on `halt` and when the controller restarts. Propose again after any of these.

`propose` refuses with a cause when the caller is not a chat process of a live session, when a plan
check fails, when an earlier run is still active, or when the chat has proposed too often in the last
minute (`chat.propose_per_min`). A refusal is not an error to work around: tell the operator the
cause. Replacing a run is the operator's: `arm --replace` from the operator's CLI.

## Read a run

`pulse-factory status [<run>]` prints the run, its state, any halt or degraded reason, the notes of
the last tick, each unit with its stage and status, each session with its tokens and cost, and the
run's total. The default run is the latest. Add `--json` for the fields by name.

A **parked** unit shows its reason. Every park opens a request, and the operator answers it in the
same run (next section). Nothing needs a new run.

## Answer a parked unit

1. `pulse-factory requests` lists the open requests, each with its kind, its unit and what it blocks.
   `pulse-factory show <R-n>` prints one: its reason, and its body. A `gaps` request holds the gap
   list the seat wrote. A `stop` request holds the stop file's text. Both are the seat's words, shown
   as data.
2. `pulse-factory claim` makes this session the one that may answer. It writes the token to a file
   and prints the generation. A new claim fences the old one out.
3. Decide with the operator, then use `answer` or `clear`:

   ```bash
   pulse-factory answer <R-n> --rev <k> --text "<the ruling>"   # records the ruling and resumes the unit
   pulse-factory clear <run> <item> [--to <stage>]              # resumes the unit with no ruling
   ```

   `--rev` is the revision that `show` printed. A request with an `on_answer` hook in the workflow
   file runs that hook first. In the `ossify-spine` workflow, a `gaps` answer is appended to the
   handoff's `## Clarifications`, and the item runs `implement` again, within the cap of 3 dispatches.
   A `stop` answer is appended to the unit's `rulings.md`, and the stop file is renamed. A hook that
   fails leaves the request answered and parks the unit again, with `answer hook failed:` and the
   cause as the reason of a new request. `clear` runs no hook.

`claim`, `answer`, `clear` and `ack` refuse a caller that is, or descends from, a seat.

## Merge the spine PR

When every item has merged and the lane has written `rounds.done`, the `spine` seat runs the first
pass of the method's spine close. It pushes the spine branch and opens the spine PR into the base
branch. Then the controller opens a `merge_ack` request for it. Nothing merges until the claim
holder acks.

1. `pulse-factory requests` lists the `merge_ack` request. `pulse-factory show <R-n>` prints the PR,
   the base branch, the head branch and the head SHA the ack will merge. Check them against the
   forge. Review the PR and drive it to a mergeable state as you would any PR.
2. `pulse-factory claim`, if this session does not hold the claim.
3. `pulse-factory ack <R-n> --rev <k>`, with the revision that `show` printed. The controller reads
   the PR again. If the head moved, it revises the request to the new SHA and refuses; `show` the
   request and ack the new revision. If the checks are not green, or the PR has a conflict, or the
   base or head branch changed, it refuses with the cause and the request stays open. Otherwise it
   merges the PR with that SHA pinned, then fetches the base branch.
4. After the merge, run the second pass in your own session or in the project's Orchestrator chat:
   `/ossify:close <spine>` on Claude Code, `skill://close <spine>` on OMP. It finds the merged PR and records the close, runs the
   demo and runs the harvest. A seat does not run it. The run ends when the method records the
   spine as closed, and `status` shows each session's cost and the run's total.

`ack` answers only a `merge_ack` request. `answer` and `clear` refuse one and name `ack`. A merge
that does not land parks the unit with a `merge_failed` request. `clear` sends it back to the merge,
which opens a new `merge_ack`. A halted or ended run refuses the ack.

## Register a project

A project is a directory the operator works in: a git repo or a plain folder. It has an ID, a name
and one root, and nothing more yet. These verbs launch nothing and change no run.

```bash
pulse-factory project add ~/projects/pulse-factory            # project P-1 added: pulse-factory (…)
pulse-factory project add ./notes --name "Field notes"        # a relative root is taken from here
pulse-factory project list                                    # P-1  pulse-factory  <HOME>
pulse-factory project remove P-2                              # the row stays; the ID is not reused
```

1. `project add <root>` records the root, made canonical, under a name. The name is the root's last
   component unless `--name` gives one. A missing path, a file, `/`, a root that a live project holds
   already, and a name that a live project holds already are refused, each with its reason. A root
   that is a linked worktree (add its main worktree instead), a bare repository, the inside of a
   `.git` directory and a repository that git refuses for dubious ownership are refused too, with
   the cause.
2. `project list` shows the live projects in creation order. `--json` gives
   `{"schema_version": 1, "projects": [...]}`.
3. A retry of `add` or `remove` sends the same `--command-id`. The controller admits the command
   once and returns the first record, with `"replayed": true`. With no `--command-id`, each call
   makes a random one.

Every `add` and `remove`, admitted or refused, is one line of `<state dir>/controller.ledger`. A seat
cannot `add` or `remove`; it can `list`.

## Chat with a project's Orchestrator

Each project has a built-in Orchestrator: a Claude Code chat that runs in the project's main worktree
on this server. You start it, send it messages, answer its approvals and questions, and end it. No
verb waits for a reply: a verb sends one request, prints one answer and exits. You read the chat with
`session items`, and the app reads it on the API stream.

```bash
pulse-factory session start --project P-1            # session S-1 started in <HOME> (worktree W-1)
pulse-factory session send S-1 "what is open?"       # sent to S-1
pulse-factory session items S-1                      # one line for each item, after --after <seq>
pulse-factory session answer S-1 4 --deny "not now"  # or --allow, or --answer "<question>=<label>"
pulse-factory session set S-1 --effort medium        # this chat only; the agent's defaults stay
pulse-factory session interrupt S-1                  # ends the running turn
pulse-factory session list                           # the live sessions, with their holders and cost
pulse-factory session end S-1                        # stops the process and ends the session
pulse-factory session redact S-1 4                   # redacts one stored item; CLI only
```

1. `chat-runtime install` fetches the managed Claude Code copy at the pinned version. The install
   script runs it. A start before it is refused with a message that names it.
2. `session start` opens the process at once. The chat uses no token until you send a message. A
   second live Orchestrator for one project is refused, and the refusal names the live `S-<n>`.
3. `session send` opens the process again when it was released or stopped, and resumes the same
   conversation. A turn begins only on your message or when a background task the chat started
   finishes. The chat cannot wake itself: no timer, tick or notice starts a turn.
4. A process with no running turn, no background task and no pending request is released after 30
   idle minutes. The next `send` resumes it. The cap is `PF_CHAT_MAX_LIVE` (default 4). A refused
   open names every live chat and why it holds its process.
5. `session answer <S-n> <seq>` answers the pending approval or question whose item has that `seq`,
   which `session items` shows.
6. A session marked `context lost` cannot resume: end it and start a new one. `halt` stops every
   live chat process, and each session stays live; the next `send` reopens it.
7. A seat, and a chat process or anything that descends from one, cannot run the state-changing
   `session` verbs. `session list` and `session items` are reads. A paired device calls `session
   list`, `start`, `send`, `answer`, `interrupt`, `set` and `end`; `redact`, `items` and `halt` are
   not open to it.

Every state-changing verb is one line of `<state dir>/controller.ledger`, and each process open,
turn and stop is one line of `<state dir>/chat.ledger`. A `send` line holds the byte count and never
the text.

## Read and set chat policies

`pulse-factory settings get [<key>] [--project P-n] [--agent <id>]` prints the value of a chat
policy for a context, with the scope it comes from. A chat reads its own policies this way.

```bash
pulse-factory settings get                                  # one line for each key
pulse-factory settings get chat.propose_per_min --project P-1
pulse-factory settings set chat.self_turn_cap 5 --project P-1   # the operator's CLI or a device
pulse-factory settings unset chat.self_turn_cap --project P-1
```

1. The keys are `chat.self_turn_cap`, `chat.deny_commands` and `chat.propose_per_min`. The last one
   bounds the proposals one chat session may build in a minute. It is a whole number from 0 to 60,
   the built-in value is 4, and `0` turns the bound off.
2. `settings set` and `settings unset` are the operator's: the CLI, and a paired device. A chat
   process, and anything that descends from one, is refused on both. Tell the operator what you
   want changed, and let them change it.
3. A retry of `set` or `unset` sends the same `--command-id`, as for `project`.

## Pair a device

The controller can serve a network API over TLS (ADR-0012). It is off until the operator sets
`PF_API_LISTEN` (`docs/install.md`). A paired device calls the project verbs, the chat verbs, `requests`,
`show`, `confirm_code`, `answer`, `clear`, `ack`, the settings verbs and `arm` with a confirm code
from a start card. `claim` and `halt` stay off it. It reads a chat on the stream
(`docs/contracts/api.md`).

```bash
pulse-factory api status          # off | waiting for <addr> | listening on <addr> | failed: <why>
pulse-factory device pair         # prints one code, and when it stops working
pulse-factory device list         # D-1  <name>  paired …  last seen … from <peer>
pulse-factory device revoke D-1   # the device's next call is refused
```

1. `device pair` prints one `pf1-` code. It works once, it expires after 10 minutes, and a new code
   replaces the live one. The code is a secret: give it to the operator, who types it into the
   device. Do not write it to a file, a ledger, a request or a message to anyone else.
2. `device list` shows each device with its pairing time, its last call and the peer address of that
   call. A revoked device is listed last, with its revoke time. `--json` gives
   `{"schema_version": 1, "devices": [...]}`. A record never holds a token.
3. `device revoke <id>` refuses that device's next call at once. The device pairs again with a new
   code. A retry sends the same `--command-id`, as for `project`.
4. `api status` says whether the API is `off`, `waiting for` an address that is not on the host yet,
   `listening on` it, or `failed`. It also prints the SPKI hash of the server key. A lost key means
   a new hash: revoke every device and pair again.

Each `device pair` redeem and each `device revoke` is one line of `<state dir>/controller.ledger`.
The line names the device and never the code or the token. A seat cannot run `device pair` or
`device revoke`; `device list` and `api status` are reads.

## Halt a run

`pulse-factory halt [<run>] --reason "<why>"` stops new launches and new merges. Seats that run
finish their stage. A repeat is safe, and the first reason stays. `halt` also stops every live chat
process and answers with the sessions it stopped (see "Chat with a project's Orchestrator").

## Other verbs

- `pulse-factory controller` runs the controller in the foreground. The systemd user unit runs it.
  You do not run it yourself.
- `pulse-factory hook` judges one tool call of a seat. The seat's extension runs it. You do not run
  it yourself.

A seat cannot arm or halt a run, it cannot add or remove a project, it cannot start or drive a chat,
and it cannot pair or revoke a device: those verbs refuse when `PF_SEAT_TOKEN` is set. A chat cannot
arm a run or change a setting: it proposes the start and the operator confirms it.
